# 4-Week Postpartum On-Ramp Block (Weeks 10–14 Postpartum)

## Client Context & Guiding Principles

She's now cleared for moderate exercise but still 4 weeks out from jumping. Coming off your earlier 4-week postpartum foundation block, she should have basic breath/core/pelvic floor coordination already. This block bridges from rehab-style work into actual strength training. Priorities in order:

1. Continue breath-to-pelvic-floor connection under load
2. Screen and progress around diastasis recti (DR) — watch for doming on every new exercise
3. Build tissue tolerance gradually before adding intensity
4. Reintroduce hinge, squat, push, pull, carry patterns under light load
5. No impact, no breath-holding, no max-effort intra-abdominal pressure

**Session length:** 30–40 minutes. **Frequency:** 3 sessions/week + 2 walks. **Equipment:** light DBs (assume she has ~5, 10, 15 lb pairs), a chair, mat, and a wall.

**Stop signs each session:** coning/doming of the linea alba, heaviness in the pelvic floor, leaking, low back pain, bleeding changes, mastitis flare. Any of these → regress or rest.

---

## WEEK 1 — Acclimatisation

Not a full programme. The goal is to expose her body to structured movement again, recalibrate exertion tolerance, and confirm what she can do without symptoms. Keep RPE 4–5/10. Long rests. No DBs heavier than 5 lb this week.

### Session A — Movement Screen + Reconnection (Mon)
- 360° breathing, supine, 2 × 8 breaths
- Heel slides with exhale-on-effort, 2 × 6/side
- Glute bridge (bodyweight), 2 × 8 — check for doming
- Bodyweight box squat to chair, 2 × 8
- Wall push-up, 2 × 8
- Side-lying clamshell, 2 × 10/side
- Dead bug (heels only, no DB), 2 × 6/side
- Finish: 5 min slow walk + diaphragmatic breathing

### Session B — Light Patterning (Wed)
- Cat-cow, 1 × 8
- Hip hinge to wall (bodyweight), 2 × 8
- Suitcase hold, 5 lb, 2 × 20 sec/side (carry pattern intro)
- Tall kneeling overhead press, 5 lb, 2 × 8
- Bird dog (slow, exhale on extension), 2 × 6/side
- Standing band/DB row mimicry, 5 lb, 2 × 10
- Finish: child's pose, 90/90 hip switches × 6

### Session C — Mini Full-Body (Fri)
- Goblet squat to chair, 5 lb, 2 × 8
- Incline push-up (counter or chair), 2 × 6
- Standing single-arm row, 5 lb, 2 × 8/side
- Glute bridge with march, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 15 sec/side
- Finish: 10 min walk

**End of Week 1 check-in:** Any leaking, doming, heaviness, low back/SI pain? Bleeding changes? Energy and sleep status? Use this to decide whether Week 2 progresses or repeats.

---

## WEEK 2 — Build Movement Quality Under Load

Assuming Week 1 went symptom-free, introduce slightly heavier DBs (up to 10 lb), longer time under tension, and a proper A/B split. RPE 5–6.

### Day 1 — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet box squat, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- DB RDL, 10 lb each, 3 × 8 (focus: exhale on the way up, no breath-holding)
- Reverse lunge, bodyweight or 5 lb, 2 × 6/side
- Glute bridge, 2 × 12
- Dead bug with arm reach, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank, knees, 2 × 20 sec/side

### Day 2 — Upper + Carries (B)
- DB floor press, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- Single-arm bent-over row, 10 lb, 3 × 8/side
- Half-kneeling overhead press, 5–10 lb, 2 × 8/side
- Suitcase carry, 10 lb, 3 × 30 sec/side
- Wall slide / scap retraction, 2 × 10
- Bird dog, 2 × 8/side

### Day 3 — Full Body (A/B hybrid)
- Goblet squat, 10 lb, 2 × 10
- Incline push-up, 2 × 8
- DB RDL, 10 lb, 2 × 10
- Single-arm row, 10 lb, 2 × 10/side
- Pallof press (band or DB held at chest), 2 × 8/side
- 10 min brisk walk

---

## WEEK 3 — Progress Load & Pattern Complexity

Introduce split stance, longer carries, slightly heavier load (up to 15 lb on hinges/squats if symptom-free). RPE 6. Still no jumping, no crunching, no plank from toes unless DR has fully closed.

### Day 1 — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet squat, 12–15 lb, 3 × 8
- DB RDL, 12–15 lb each, 3 × 8
- Split squat, 5–10 lb DBs, 2 × 8/side
- Glute bridge with 10 lb on hips, 3 × 10
- Dead bug with opposite arm + leg, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 25 sec/side

### Day 2 — Upper + Carries (B)
- DB floor press, 12 lb, 3 × 10
- Chest-supported row (over chair/bench), 10–12 lb, 3 × 10
- Standing overhead press, 8–10 lb, 3 × 8
- Suitcase carry, 12–15 lb, 3 × 40 sec/side
- Bent-over reverse fly, 5 lb, 2 × 10
- Bird dog, 2 × 8/side, slowed tempo

### Day 3 — Full Body Circuit (90 sec rest between rounds)
3 rounds of:
- Goblet squat × 8 (12 lb)
- Push-up (incline as needed) × 8
- DB RDL × 8 (12 lb)
- Single-arm row × 8/side (12 lb)
- Pallof press × 8/side

---

## WEEK 4 — Consolidate & Test Readiness for Impact

Final week before her jumping clearance. Goal: confirm she can tolerate higher load and impact-prep work (low-level plyometric *precursors* only — no actual jumps yet). RPE 6–7.

### Day 1 — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet squat, 15 lb, 4 × 8
- DB RDL, 15 lb each, 4 × 8
- Split squat, 10 lb DBs, 3 × 8/side
- Step-up to low step, 10 lb, 2 × 8/side
- Heel raises (calf prep for landing), 3 × 12
- Side plank from knees with top leg lift, 2 × 8/side
- Dead bug, 2 × 8/side

### Day 2 — Upper + Carries (B)
- DB bench (floor) press, 15 lb, 4 × 8
- Single-arm row, 15 lb, 4 × 8/side
- Standing OH press, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- Farmer carry (both hands), 15 lb each, 3 × 45 sec
- Half-kneeling Pallof, 3 × 8/side
- Bird dog row, 8–10 lb, 2 × 6/side

### Day 3 — Full Body + Impact Prep
- Goblet squat, 15 lb, 3 × 10
- Push-up (knees or full if DR closed), 3 × 6–8
- DB RDL, 15 lb, 3 × 10
- Single-arm row, 15 lb, 3 × 10/side
- **Impact prep block** (no jumping yet):
  - Marching in place, 2 × 30 sec
  - Heel raise to forefoot hop *simulation* (stay on ground, fast contraction), 2 × 10
  - Fast step-back to lunge (no bounce), 2 × 6/side
- Pallof press, 2 × 10/side

---

## End-of-Block Readiness Checklist (before introducing jumping in Week 5)

Before you progress her to plyometrics, confirm:
- No leaking during fast marches, carries, or coughing/sneezing
- No pelvic heaviness during or after sessions
- DR: no doming under load; ideally <2 finger-width gap with good tension
- Tolerating 15 lb DBs across hinges/squats/rows symptom-free
- Walking 30+ min without symptoms
- Sleep and energy trending up, not down, across the block

If anything fails, hold impact for another 1–2 weeks and continue Week 4-style work. If all green, you can begin a 2-week plyometric on-ramp (pogos → low-amplitude jumps → bilateral landings → unilateral) before any running.

---

## Recovery & Lifestyle Notes

- **Walks:** 2 × 20–30 min/week on non-training days, flat terrain.
- **Sleep:** brutal at 10 weeks PP. If she had <5 hrs broken sleep, drop the session to 2 sets of each exercise and shorten to 20 min — don't cancel, just downscale.
- **Hydration:** especially if breastfeeding — 3+ L/day.
- **Nutrition:** ensure adequate protein (1.6–2.0 g/kg) and don't cut calories aggressively, particularly if lactating. This block isn't a fat-loss block.
- **Pelvic floor PT referral:** if not already done, strongly recommend at least one assessment before Week 5 impact reintroduction. Worth its weight in gold.

Let me know how Week 1 lands and we can adjust loads, or build the Week 5–8 block to layer in plyo and running prep.

# Adding Cardio to the On-Ramp Block

Good news: cardio is very doable here, and the spin background helps because she already has the pattern, the seat tolerance, and the aerobic base memory. The constraints are the same as for lifting — no impact, no breath-holding/maximal effort, watch pelvic floor symptoms, and respect that her cardiovascular deconditioning is real even if her legs remember how to pedal.

## What's Safe Right Now

**Green light (low/no impact, low pelvic floor load):**
- Stationary bike / spin bike — seated only for now
- Brisk walking, including incline walking on a treadmill
- Swimming (only once lochia has fully stopped and OB is happy — confirm)
- Elliptical
- Rower at low-moderate pace (watch posture — no aggressive lean-back)

**Yellow light (later in the block, with caveats):**
- Standing/out-of-saddle spin — wait until Week 3 minimum, and only short bursts. Standing significantly increases intra-abdominal pressure and pelvic floor demand.
- Hills on the bike at high resistance — same reasoning, keep resistance moderate.

**Red light until cleared for impact:**
- Running, jogging, jumping intervals
- HIIT classes with burpees/jumps
- Heavy sprint efforts on the bike where she'd be holding her breath

## Spin-Specific Cautions

Because she knows spin culture, flag these explicitly with her:

- **No "push to failure" or breath-holding sprints.** If she can't talk in short sentences, she's too high.
- **Stay seated this whole block.** Standing climbs load the pelvic floor heavily and are a common trigger for leaking postpartum.
- **Saddle tolerance can be different now** — perineal tissue, C-section scar pressure, or SI joint laxity may make her old saddle uncomfortable. Padded shorts, shorter sessions, and saddle position check.
- **Cap RPE at 7/10 this block.** No all-out efforts.
- **If breastfeeding:** feed or pump before harder sessions — engorgement makes anything aerobic miserable.

## How to Slot It In

She's doing 3 strength sessions + 2 walks. I'd convert one of those walks into a steady bike session and add one interval session on a non-lifting day. That gives her:

- 3 strength sessions
- 1 steady-state cardio session
- 1 interval cardio session
- 1 easy walk (keep this — it's recovery, not training)
- 1 full rest day

Total cardio load stays modest and won't compete with the strength work, especially important given sleep is still rough.

## Week-by-Week Cardio Progression

### Week 1 — Just Re-Introduce the Bike
**Goal:** sit on the bike, spin easy, confirm no symptoms. Don't chase a workout.

- **Steady ride:** 15 min, RPE 4/10, conversational. Flat resistance, comfortable cadence (80–90 rpm).
- **No intervals this week.** Replace the second cardio slot with her usual walk.

Check post-session: any leaking, heaviness, perineal soreness, scar pulling? If yes, regress to walking next week.

### Week 2 — Build Duration, Introduce Light Intervals
**Steady ride:** 20–25 min, RPE 5/10.

**Interval session (seated only):**
- 5 min easy warm-up
- 6 × (1 min moderate effort RPE 6 / 1 min easy RPE 4)
- 5 min cool-down
- Total: ~22 min

Cue her: nasal breathing during the "easy" portions to keep intensity honest.

### Week 3 — Lengthen Intervals
**Steady ride:** 25–30 min, RPE 5–6/10. Can add gentle rolling resistance changes if she wants variety, but stay seated.

**Interval session:**
- 5 min warm-up
- 5 × (2 min at RPE 6–7 / 90 sec easy)
- 5 min cool-down
- Total: ~28 min

If symptom-free and she wants more spin "feel," she can do *very brief* (10–15 sec) out-of-saddle positions on the easy portions just to change posture — not as work intervals. Skip if any pelvic symptoms.

### Week 4 — Test Aerobic Capacity Before Impact Phase
**Steady ride:** 30 min, RPE 6/10.

**Interval session — Spin-style pyramid:**
- 5 min warm-up
- 1 min / 2 min / 3 min / 2 min / 1 min at RPE 6–7, with equal rest between
- 5 min cool-down
- Total: ~30 min

This gives her a satisfying spin-feel session and lets you assess her readiness for the higher-intensity work and impact reintroduction in Week 5.

## Weekly Schedule (Updated)

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Strength Day 1 (Lower + Core) |
| Tue | Steady bike |
| Wed | Strength Day 2 (Upper + Carries) |
| Thu | Easy walk 20–30 min |
| Fri | Strength Day 3 (Full Body) |
| Sat | Bike intervals |
| Sun | Rest |

Flex it around her week — order matters less than spacing the harder sessions. The one rule: **don't put bike intervals the day before or after Lower Day** in Weeks 3–4, as leg fatigue will degrade squat/RDL quality.

## Symptom Watch for Cardio Specifically

Same stop signs as lifting, plus:
- Leaking on the bike (common signal that intensity is too high or position is loading the pelvic floor)
- Pelvic heaviness during or in the hours after a ride
- New perineal pain or scar discomfort
- Resting HR jumping 10+ bpm above her recent baseline the next morning (sign she's overcooking it given sleep deficit)

If any of these show up, regress to steady-state only for a week, then retry intervals.

## A Note on Expectations

Set this up front with her: **her aerobic capacity will feel embarrassingly low compared to her pre-pregnancy spin fitness.** That's normal. Relaxin is still circulating (especially if breastfeeding), blood volume and stroke volume are recalibrating, and sleep is fragmented. Telling her now prevents her from chasing old numbers and pushing into red-flag territory. The fitness will come back — quickly, given her base — but the first 4–6 weeks of cardio should feel almost too easy.

Let me know if she wants more cardio volume than this (some postpartum clients crave it for mental health reasons and we can absolutely accommodate), or if she'd rather front-load strength and keep cardio minimal. Either is fine, this is just my default split.

# Core Component — Anti-Flexion Focus

Good call. Crunches and sit-ups are the wrong tool here for two reasons: they load the linea alba in exactly the direction that perpetuates DR, and they teach a flexion-dominant strategy that does nothing for the load-bearing demands of motherhood (carrying baby, car seats, prams, lifting from the floor). What she actually needs is the ability to **resist** unwanted spinal movement under load — anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion — while breathing.

Some of this is already woven into the programme (dead bugs, bird dogs, Pallof, carries, side planks). This adds a dedicated, progressive core block she does either as a finisher on strength days or as a short standalone.

## Principles

- **Breathe through everything.** Exhale on effort, no Valsalva. If she's holding her breath, the load is too high or the position is wrong.
- **Watch the linea alba** on every rep — if you see doming or coning, regress immediately.
- **Quality over reps.** 5 perfect reps beats 15 sloppy ones, always, but especially now.
- **No spinal flexion under load** this block. No crunches, no sit-ups, no V-ups, no Russian twists, no toes-to-bar.
- **Plank from toes only when DR has closed and she can hold without doming.** Knees are not a regression to be ashamed of — they're the right call for most clients at 10 weeks PP.

## The Four Categories

1. **Anti-extension** — resisting the lower back arching (dead bugs, hollow holds eventually, plank variations)
2. **Anti-rotation** — resisting trunk rotation (Pallof press, bird dog, half-kneeling chops later)
3. **Anti-lateral flexion** — resisting side bend (side plank, suitcase carry)
4. **Anti-extension + load transfer** — bracing while limbs move under load (bird dog rows, dead bug with DB, loaded carries)

Every week she should hit at least one from each category.

## Week-by-Week Core Block

Add **5–8 minutes at the end of each strength session**, rotating focus. Cue every rep: *"exhale, ribs down, lengthen through the crown."*

### Week 1 — Reconnection
Focus: find the brace, no load, master the breath.

**Day 1 (after Lower):**
- 90/90 supine breathing with exhale-brace, 2 × 6 breaths
- Dead bug, heels only, 2 × 6/side
- Side-lying breathing into the obliques, 1 × 5/side

**Day 2 (after Upper):**
- Bird dog, slow, 2 × 6/side
- Pallof press, light band or 5 lb DB at chest, 2 × 8/side
- Wall plank (hands on wall, lean in), 2 × 20 sec

**Day 3 (after Full Body):**
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 15 sec/side
- Dead bug, 2 × 6/side
- Suitcase hold, 5 lb, 2 × 20 sec/side

### Week 2 — Add Limb Load & Time

**Day 1:**
- Dead bug with arm reach (alternating), 3 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 20 sec/side
- Bird dog, paused 2 sec at extension, 2 × 8/side

**Day 2:**
- Half-kneeling Pallof press, 3 × 8/side
- Bear hold (hands and knees hover, knees 1 inch off floor), 2 × 15 sec
- Suitcase carry, 10 lb, 2 × 30 sec/side

**Day 3:**
- Side plank from knees with reach-through, 2 × 6/side
- Dead bug with opposite arm + leg, 2 × 6/side
- Pallof press hold, 2 × 20 sec/side

### Week 3 — Add External Load & Asymmetry

**Day 1:**
- Dead bug holding 5 lb DB in straight arms (arms stay vertical, legs march), 3 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees with top leg lift, 2 × 8/side
- Bird dog, 3 × 8/side

**Day 2:**
- Tall-kneeling Pallof press, 3 × 10/side
- Bear hold with shoulder tap, 2 × 6/side
- Single-arm farmer carry (suitcase), 12 lb, 3 × 40 sec/side

**Day 3:**
- Side plank from knees, full duration build, 2 × 30 sec/side
- Bird dog row, 5 lb, 2 × 6/side
- Half-kneeling chop (band or light DB, high-to-low), 2 × 8/side

### Week 4 — Test Tolerance, Add Dynamic Demand

This is the readiness week — these exercises should tell you whether her core is ready for plyometric demand in the next block. If she can do these without doming, leaking, or symptoms, she's likely ready for impact.

**Day 1:**
- Dead bug with 8–10 lb DB, 3 × 8/side
- Side plank from feet (if DR closed and no doming), 2 × 20 sec/side — *otherwise stay on knees, 30 sec/side*
- Bird dog with 2-sec pause + slow return, 3 × 8/side

**Day 2:**
- Half-kneeling Pallof press with slow tempo (3 sec out, 1 sec hold, 3 sec in), 3 × 8/side
- Bear crawl, slow forward + back, 2 × 4 steps each direction
- Farmer carry, 15 lb each hand, 3 × 45 sec

**Day 3:**
- Side plank with hip dip (small ROM), 2 × 8/side
- Bird dog row, 8 lb, 3 × 8/side
- Tall-kneeling anti-rotation hold (Pallof position, hold 20 sec), 2 × 20 sec/side

## Key Coaching Cues

- **"Exhale as you do the hard part."** Every rep.
- **"Ribs down, ribs over hips."** Stops the flared-rib, pelvic-tilt cheat that hides core dysfunction.
- **"If you can't breathe, you can't brace."** If she's gripping and holding her breath, regress.
- **"Long, not crunched."** Cue length through the body rather than shortening.
- **"Watch your belly."** Get her watching her own midline for doming — it's a skill she'll use forever.

## What to Watch For

- **Doming/coning** along the linea alba → regress immediately (drop a limb, shorten lever, reduce load)
- **Lower back arching** during dead bugs → her ribs are flaring; cue exhale and ribs down, or shorten the leg lever
- **Hip shifting/twisting** during bird dog → too much range, slow it down
- **Leaking during Pallof or carries** → load is too high or she's bracing without exhaling
- **Pelvic heaviness later in the day** → reduce volume next session

## End-of-Block Core Benchmark

By end of Week 4, symptom-free, you'd ideally like to see:
- 8 reps/side dead bug with 10 lb DB, no doming
- 30 sec side plank from feet, no hip sag (or 45 sec from knees if feet aren't appropriate yet)
- Farmer carry 15 lb/hand for 45 sec with upright posture
- Pallof press 10 reps/side with slow tempo and steady breath

If she hits those without symptoms, her core is ready for the impact reintroduction block. If not, hold her here another 1–2 weeks — there's no rush, and a robust deep core will pay off through every block you write her this year.

Let me know if you want me to build the Week 5–8 block now, or wait until you've seen how she handles this one.

# Diastasis Recti Screening for Your Client

Since she hasn't been formally assessed, you'll want to do this yourself before you load her further — and then re-screen every 2 weeks through this block. It's not complicated, but the *quality* of what you're looking for matters more than the gap measurement itself.

**Important caveat upfront:** you're a trainer, not a clinician. You're screening for function and identifying red flags that warrant referral — you're not diagnosing or treating. If you find anything concerning, refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist. Frame this with her the same way.

## What Diastasis Actually Is

Diastasis recti abdominis (DRA) is a widening and thinning of the linea alba — the connective tissue running down the midline of the abdomen between the two sides of the rectus. It's *normal and universal* in late pregnancy. The question at 10 weeks postpartum isn't "does she have one?" — most women still do to some degree — it's:

1. How wide is the gap?
2. **More importantly: can she generate tension across the linea alba?**

Modern thinking has shifted away from gap width as the headline measure. A 3-finger gap with good tension and no doming is functionally better than a 1.5-finger gap with no tension and a squishy, bulging midline. **Function > gap.**

## The Screen — Step by Step

Do this with her lying supine, knees bent, feet flat, head supported by a pillow or your hand. Shirt up so you can see the midline. Get her permission and explain what you're doing each step.

### Step 1: Visual Assessment at Rest
Look at her relaxed abdomen. Note:
- Any visible bulging or doming along the midline at rest
- Asymmetry between left and right sides
- Scar location/quality if C-section

### Step 2: The Lift Test (Gap Measurement)
1. Ask her to exhale and gently lift her head and shoulders off the floor — just to where her shoulder blades barely clear. **Not a full sit-up.**
2. As she lifts, place your fingers horizontally (perpendicular to the midline) at three locations:
   - **2–3 cm above the navel**
   - **At the navel**
   - **2–3 cm below the navel**
3. At each point, press gently down into the abdomen and feel for the edges of the rectus on either side. Measure the gap in **finger widths**.
4. Note the **depth** — does your finger sink in barely, or several knuckles deep? Depth often matters more than width.

**Record both width and depth at all three points.** A gap can be wider above the navel and tight below, or vice versa. Document it.

### Step 3: The Tension Test (The Important One)
This is what most people skip and it's the most useful information you'll get.

1. Same position. Fingers at the navel.
2. Ask her to **exhale gently and engage her deep core** ("draw your belly button gently toward your spine" or "exhale like blowing out birthday candles") *before* lifting her head.
3. Then lift the head with the brace engaged.
4. Feel: **does the linea alba become taut under your fingers, or does it stay soft/squishy?**

- **Taut and trampoline-like under the fingers** = she can generate tension. Good sign, even if a gap exists.
- **Soft, squishy, fingers sink deeply** = poor tension generation. This is the bigger concern, regardless of gap width.

### Step 4: The Doming/Coning Test
With her in the same position:
1. Ask her to lift her head **without** the pre-brace — just a normal small crunch motion.
2. Watch the midline carefully. Does a **ridge or dome** push up along the linea alba? Sometimes it's subtle — look for a football-shaped bulge from sternum to pubic bone.
3. Then ask her to try again **with** the exhale-brace strategy. Does the doming reduce or disappear?

If she can prevent doming with the right breath strategy, that's actionable — she has a tool. If she domes regardless of strategy, the load is too high for her current capacity and you need to regress.

## What the Findings Mean

| Finding | Interpretation | Action |
|---|---|---|
| <2 finger gap, good tension, no doming | Functionally resolved or near-resolved | Progress normally |
| 2–3 finger gap, good tension, no doming | Common at 10 wks PP, functionally okay | Progress with continued screening |
| Any gap with **poor tension** (squishy/deep) | Connective tissue not load-ready | Stay in current phase, prioritise breath + deep core, **refer to pelvic PT** |
| Visible doming under load | Current load exceeds her capacity | Regress that specific exercise |
| Gap >3 fingers anywhere | Significant DR | **Refer to pelvic PT** before progressing load |
| Any bulging at rest | Possible hernia (especially at umbilicus) | **Refer to GP/OB** before continuing |

## Red Flags — Refer Out Immediately

- **Visible bulge at the navel at rest**, especially if it gets bigger when she coughs or strains → possible umbilical hernia, needs medical assessment
- **Pain along the midline** during exertion
- **Pelvic floor symptoms** (leaking, heaviness, prolapse sensation) alongside DR → pelvic floor PT, ideally before more loading
- **Low back or SI pain** that's worsening with the programme
- **Gap >3 fingers** that hasn't narrowed by Week 4 of your block
- **Inability to generate any tension** across the midline despite coaching

## How to Screen During Sessions (Ongoing)

You won't do the full supine screen every session — that's overkill. But you should be **visually screening on every loaded core or compound exercise.** Specifically:

- **Dead bugs:** watch the midline as the leg extends. Doming = regress the lever.
- **Bird dog:** watch from the side. Low back arching or midline doming = regress.
- **Plank variations:** look down the body from her head. Any tenting along the midline = regress.
- **Loaded carries:** watch from the front. Any bulging while she walks = load too heavy or breath strategy wrong.
- **Squats and RDLs:** less obvious, but watch for doming on the concentric phase. This is where breath-holding under load shows up.
- **Push-ups:** the midline is fully visible — easy to spot doming.

Get her to **self-screen too.** Have her check her own midline in the mirror or by looking down during exercises. By Week 4 she should be able to identify doming on herself — it's a skill she'll need beyond this block.

## Formal Re-screens

Schedule a full supine screen at:
- **Start of Week 1** (baseline)
- **Start of Week 3**
- **End of Week 4** (readiness assessment for next block)

Document each one — gap width and depth at three points, tension quality, doming response with and without brace strategy. This gives you data to make decisions on, not vibes, and it shows her tangible progress (which is motivating when the scale isn't moving and she's exhausted).

## What to Tell Her

Frame this for her plainly:
- DR is normal — almost every postpartum woman has one at 10 weeks
- The goal isn't to "close the gap" — it's to build a midline that can generate tension and tolerate load
- Some women's gaps fully close, some don't, and *function matters more than the number*
- You're screening so you can train her safely, not because something is wrong
- If you find anything that needs more expertise than yours, you'll refer her — that's normal and protective, not a setback

## Referral Threshold — A Practical Rule

When in doubt, refer. A single appointment with a pelvic floor physio is worth more than weeks of guessing. If you're in a position to suggest one specifically, build that relationship now — postpartum clients are a significant chunk of most trainers' books, and having a pelvic PT you trust on speed dial makes you better at your job.

Let me know what the baseline screen shows when you do it, and we can adjust the rest of the block accordingly — particularly the core work and any loading thresholds.

# Pushing Intensity in Week 2 — Carefully

Short answer: yes, but selectively, and we don't tear up the plan. "Feeling great" at 10–11 weeks postpartum is excellent news but it's also exactly when clients (and trainers) get themselves into trouble. The tissue takes longer to remodel than the nervous system takes to feel ready. Relaxin is still circulating (especially if breastfeeding), the linea alba is still remodelling, and sleep is still fragmented — meaning recovery capacity is lower than her perceived energy suggests.

So we'll progress, but with rules.

## The Rules for Progressing Her Now

1. **Progress one variable at a time per session.** Load OR reps OR complexity — never two at once. This is how you spot what causes a symptom if one appears.
2. **No progression on any exercise that showed doming, leaking, or heaviness in Week 1.** Those exercises stay at Week 2 prescription until clean.
3. **Cap RPE at 6/10** for the rest of Week 2, 7/10 for Week 3. We are not chasing failure this block.
4. **The screen still rules.** If you see doming when she moves to a heavier DB, the DB goes back down. Her feelings don't override the visual.
5. **Recovery markers are non-negotiable.** If resting HR is up, sleep dropped, or she feels heaviness later in the day, we hold or regress next session.

## What to Push (and What Not To)

### Safe to push now
- **Load on hinge patterns** (RDL) — she's well-positioned, hinges tolerate load well, and this is where she'll feel the most "training" effect for the least risk.
- **Load on rows** — very low pelvic floor / midline risk, easy win.
- **Carry duration and load** — the most postpartum-appropriate intensity progression that exists. Heavy carries build core, grip, posture, and conditioning simultaneously.
- **Time under tension** on squats and presses — slower tempos before heavier loads.
- **Cardio intervals** — within the cap I set (RPE 7), she can absolutely earn more here.

### Hold steady for now
- **Squat load** — progress modestly, but the squat loads the pelvic floor more than the hinge. Don't jump it.
- **Overhead pressing load** — overhead loading increases intra-abdominal pressure significantly. Small jumps only.
- **Plank progressions** — keep these on the planned timeline. Doming risk is highest here.

### Do not push yet
- **Impact** — no. Four weeks PP rule from OB stands. We're not negotiating this regardless of how good she feels.
- **Standing/out-of-saddle spin** — same reasoning as last message. Pelvic floor load is too high too soon.
- **Anything explosive** — no kettlebell swings, no jump squats, no plyo precursors at full intensity yet.
- **True flexion-based core** — still no.

## Revised Rest of Week 2

The Day 1 you've already done stays as written. Adjust Day 2 and Day 3:

### Day 2 — Upper + Carries (revised, mid-Week 2)
- DB floor press, **12 lb**, 3 × 8 *(up from 10)*
- Single-arm bent-over row, **12 lb**, 3 × 10/side *(up from 10 lb × 8)*
- Half-kneeling overhead press, 10 lb, 3 × 8/side *(extra set, same load)*
- Suitcase carry, **12 lb**, 3 × 40 sec/side *(up from 10 lb × 30 sec)*
- Wall slide / scap retraction, 2 × 10
- Bird dog, 2 × 8/side, **2-sec pause at extension** *(complexity bump, same load)*

### Day 3 — Full Body (revised)
- Goblet squat, 12 lb, 3 × 8 *(extra set, modest load bump)*
- Incline push-up, **slightly lower surface**, 3 × 8 *(complexity, not load)*
- DB RDL, **12 lb**, 3 × 10
- Single-arm row, 12 lb, 3 × 10/side
- Pallof press, **3 × 10/side** with 2-sec hold at full extension
- 10–15 min brisk walk

That's a real progression — more total work, modestly heavier where it's safest — without rewriting the block.

## Updated Week 3 (Pulling Forward Selectively)

If she finishes the revised Week 2 symptom-free, Week 3 progresses as originally written **except**:

- RDL can go to **15 lb** rather than 12–15 — give her the real bump
- Carries can go to **15 lb** for 45 sec
- Add a **fourth strength day** as an option if she's craving more: a short 20-min full-body circuit at moderate load on what was the rest day. Only do this if she's sleeping >5 hrs broken and not flagging by midweek.

Don't pull Week 4 forward. Week 4 is the readiness test for impact, and we need a full week of consolidation before that assessment is meaningful. Compressing the block undermines the whole point of an on-ramp.

## Cardio Progression

She can also push here. For the rest of Week 2:

- **Steady ride:** extend to 25–30 min at RPE 5–6
- **Intervals:** bump to 8 × (1 min RPE 6 / 1 min easy) instead of the planned 6 rounds

Week 3 intervals can go to **6 × (2 min RPE 7 / 90 sec easy)** if she's tolerating well.

## The Conversation to Have With Her

Tell her explicitly:
- "Feeling great is exactly when postpartum clients get hurt. The reason isn't your effort — it's that connective tissue heals on its own timeline, not your motivation's."
- "We're going to give you more work, but we're not collapsing the timeline. The plyometric block is still Week 5+."
- "If anything I'm watching for shows up — doming, leaking, heaviness, a bad night of sleep that turns into two — we hold. That's not a setback, it's the plan working."

Postpartum clients who feel good in Week 2 often want to act like they're back to normal by Week 4. Set the expectation now that the on-ramp exists *because* she's going to feel ready before she actually is. Your job is to give her enough stimulus to feel like she's training, while protecting her from the version of herself that would do too much.

## What to Watch For Over the Next 7–10 Days

- **Late-day pelvic heaviness** — a classic "too much, too soon" signal. Often shows up that evening, not during the session.
- **Sleep dropping** further despite training feeling good — overreaching sign.
- **Resting HR up 5+ bpm** from her recent baseline — same.
- **Any new leaking**, even minor, with anything — immediate regression of whatever introduced it.
- **Doming on the heavier RDLs or carries** — drop the load.
- **Mood/irritability shift** — postpartum recovery is hormonal as well as physical; if she's overdoing it, mood often tells you before the body does.

If any of those show up, hold Week 3 at Week 2 levels and re-screen the diastasis. If none show up by end of Week 2, run Week 3 as updated and we're on track for the impact-readiness assessment at end of Week 4.

Let me know how Day 2 and Day 3 land and we'll calibrate from there.

# HIIT for Fat Loss — Let's Talk First, Then Programme

I'll give you something to work with, but I'd push back on parts of this request before we slot it in. Both the HIIT timing and the fat loss framing need adjusting before we just say yes. This is the conversation that earns you trust as her trainer — saying yes to everything she wants right now is the path to setbacks she'll blame you for later.

## Why I'm Pushing Back

### On the HIIT itself

True HIIT — the way she remembers it, with burpees, jump squats, mountain climbers, sprint intervals at near-max effort — is **not appropriate yet** for three independent reasons:

1. **Impact is still off the table until Week 5 minimum.** OB cleared her for moderate exercise, no jumping for 4 weeks. We're in Week 2. Burpees, jump squats, jumping jacks, high knees, skaters — all out.
2. **Maximal-effort intervals drive intra-abdominal pressure through the roof.** That's exactly the load the linea alba and pelvic floor are least ready for at 10–11 weeks PP. This is true even for non-impact HIIT like assault bike or rower sprints.
3. **She's already progressing well.** Adding a high-stress modality on top of a working programme is how you trigger the symptoms we've successfully avoided so far. "Feeling great in Week 2" is not the moment to introduce the highest-risk modality.

### On the fat loss framing

This one matters more than the HIIT question and I'd raise it with her directly:

- **Fat loss is the wrong primary goal at 10–11 weeks postpartum**, especially if she's breastfeeding. Aggressive calorie deficit + high training stress + fragmented sleep + lactation demands = a recipe for low milk supply, hormonal disruption, prolonged recovery, and rebound weight gain.
- **HIIT is not a particularly good fat loss tool anyway.** Energy expenditure per session is modest; the "afterburn" effect is real but small and oversold by group fitness marketing. Strength training plus walking plus a modest protein-forward calorie awareness will outperform HIIT for postpartum body composition almost every time, with a fraction of the risk.
- **Her body composition will shift over the next 6–12 months largely on its own**, as long as she's training, eating enough protein, walking, and sleeping when she can. The clients who get the best long-term postpartum results are the ones who play the long game in the first 4–6 months, not the ones who go scorched-earth at 10 weeks.

You don't need to lecture her — but you do need to redirect the framing before you give her the tool, or you'll be writing HIIT sessions she uses to punish herself.

## The Conversation to Have

Something like:

> "I hear you — and we'll get you back to HIIT, I promise. But we can't run the version you remember yet, for two reasons: jumping isn't cleared until Week 5, and all-out efforts spike pressure through your core in a way your tissue isn't ready for. What I can give you starting in Week 3 is a postpartum-appropriate version that scratches the same itch — it'll feel hard, you'll sweat, you'll get the conditioning hit — and we'll build from there. On the fat loss piece: that's coming, but the fastest path right now is the strength work plus protein plus walks, not adding more intensity. Trust me through this block and you'll be doing real HIIT by Week 8."

If she's on board, here's how we slot it in.

## What HIIT Looks Like in This Block

We're swapping the **Week 3 and Week 4 bike interval session** for a low-impact, non-Valsalva, postpartum-appropriate conditioning circuit. We are **not adding a fourth session.** Total weekly load doesn't go up — we're trading like for like.

### The Format

- **Work:rest ratios** stay conservative: 30 sec on / 30 sec off, or 40 sec on / 20 sec off — *not* 20:10 Tabata-style. Postpartum nervous systems don't need 20:10 in Week 3.
- **No impact, no jumping.**
- **No exercises that load the midline in flexion or under breath-hold** (no mountain climbers, no plank jacks, no burpees, no jumping jacks).
- **Exhale on every working rep.** This is the difference between a postpartum HIIT session and a Crossfit class.
- **Stop if doming, leaking, or heaviness shows up at any point.** Non-negotiable.

### Approved Exercise Pool

**Lower body (low-impact power substitutes):**
- Goblet squats, controlled tempo
- Reverse lunges
- DB step-ups (low step)
- Glute bridge with march
- Heel-elevated tempo squats
- KB/DB sumo deadlift, light

**Upper/full body:**
- DB push press (light, half-kneeling)
- Single-arm row, alternating
- Renegade row (if no doming — assess first)
- DB thruster, light, seated or standing
- DB clean (no jump), light
- Push-up to row (incline)

**Cardio machines (if available):**
- Stationary bike, seated, moderate-hard intervals
- Rower at moderate cadence (watch posture)
- Elliptical at high cadence

**Carries as conditioning:**
- Farmer carry intervals
- Suitcase carry intervals

Notice what's missing: anything that flexes the spine, anything that jumps, anything that demands a held breath. That's the whole game.

## Week 3 — Conditioning Circuit (Replaces Sat Bike Intervals)

5 min easy bike or brisk walk warm-up.

**Circuit — 3 rounds, 30 sec work / 30 sec rest:**
1. Goblet squat, 12 lb
2. Single-arm row, 12 lb (switch sides each round)
3. Reverse lunge, alternating, bodyweight or 5 lb
4. Half-kneeling DB push press, 8–10 lb (switch sides each round)
5. Farmer carry, 12 lb each hand, walking
6. Bike sprint, seated, RPE 7

Rest 2 min between rounds.

5 min cool-down + breathwork.

Total: ~25 min. RPE peaks at 7. She'll sweat, she'll breathe hard, she'll feel like she trained — but no impact, no Valsalva, no flexion.

## Week 4 — Conditioning Circuit (Progressed)

5 min warm-up.

**Circuit — 4 rounds, 40 sec work / 20 sec rest:**
1. Goblet squat, 15 lb
2. DB push press, 10 lb (alternating arms standing, or both arms if symptom-free)
3. DB step-up to low step, 10 lb (alternating)
4. Single-arm row, 15 lb (alternating)
5. Suitcase carry, 15 lb (switch sides each round)
6. Bike or rower, RPE 7–8

Rest 90 sec between rounds.

5 min cool-down.

Total: ~30 min. This is the closest to "real" HIIT we'll get in this block — and it should be enough to satisfy her that the modality is back on the menu.

## The Plyometric On-Ramp (Week 5+)

To give her something to look forward to: assuming the Week 4 readiness assessment goes clean (no doming under load, no leaking on conditioning, DR generating tension, all benchmarks hit), Week 5 begins reintroducing impact in a controlled order:

1. **Week 5:** pogos in place, low amplitude → low box step-downs → bilateral broad-jump landings (no jump, just stick the landing from a low step)
2. **Week 6:** small jump squats, low skater hops, jumping jacks at low intensity
3. **Week 7–8:** add running intervals (run/walk), build toward proper HIIT format
4. **Week 8+:** the HIIT class she actually wants

That's a believable runway to give her. Three to four weeks from now she can be doing the workouts she's asking for, properly, with the tissue capacity to absorb them. Three to four weeks of holding the line is nothing in the scope of her training year.

## On the Fat Loss Piece Specifically

If she's set on body composition work running in parallel, here's the postpartum-appropriate way to support it without sabotaging recovery:

- **Protein at 1.6–2.0 g/kg of goal bodyweight.** Most clients undershoot this dramatically. If she's lactating, err high.
- **Modest deficit only, and only if not breastfeeding.** If breastfeeding, no deliberate deficit at all this block. Lactation already burns 300–500 kcal/day; her body will recomp on its own with adequate training and protein.
- **Walking volume up.** Steps drive postpartum fat loss more reliably than HIIT does. Target 8–10k/day as a rolling average if it's feasible with the baby.
- **Sleep where possible.** Not actionable in the way she wants, but worth naming — sleep deprivation drives cortisol up and appetite regulation down, and undermines both training and fat loss.
- **No weigh-ins this block.** Scale weight at 10–14 weeks PP is dominated by fluid shifts, breast tissue, and hormonal fluctuation. It will frustrate her and tell her nothing useful. Use tape measurements or progress photos monthly if she wants a metric.

That's the honest version of fat loss support right now. The HIIT she's asking for is, at best, a small contributor — and at worst, the thing that derails the rest of the programme.

Let me know how she takes the conversation and how the first conditioning session lands. If she pushes back hard on the framing, that's worth knowing too — sometimes there's a body image or postpartum mental health piece sitting underneath the request that's bigger than programming and worth flagging gently.

# Return to Running — The Real Timeline

Good goal, and autumn is achievable depending on exactly when "autumn" is, but I want to set realistic expectations before you have the conversation with her. The single biggest mistake postpartum runners make — and the trainers who programme for them — is treating the OB's "cleared for moderate exercise" as clearance to run. It isn't. The OB is clearing her for *exercise*, not for the specific orthopaedic and pelvic floor demands of running, which are an order of magnitude higher than walking or strength training.

## The Honest Timeline

Current consensus from postpartum sports medicine and pelvic health research (Goom, Donnelly, Brockwell — the 2019 guidelines and subsequent work) is that **return to running should not begin before 12 weeks postpartum at the absolute earliest, and many women aren't ready until 16–20 weeks or beyond.** She's 10 weeks now.

That gives us:

- **Earliest possible first run:** ~Week 14–16 postpartum (4–6 weeks from now)
- **Realistic first run for most clients:** Week 16–20 postpartum
- **10k race-ready:** typically 4–6 months from first run, done properly

So if "autumn" means **late October or November**, a 10k is realistic with a careful build. If she's thinking **early September**, that's too aggressive and we should renegotiate the goal — or the distance.

## Why It Takes This Long

Running is roughly **2.5–3x bodyweight ground reaction force per step**, repeated 150–180 times per minute, for 30+ minutes. At 10 weeks postpartum, the tissues that absorb that load — pelvic floor, abdominal wall, hip stabilisers, plantar fascia, Achilles, tibial bone — are not at pre-pregnancy capacity. Relaxin is still circulating (longer if breastfeeding). The pelvic floor has been through significant trauma regardless of delivery mode. The abdominal wall is still remodelling.

Running before the tissues are ready doesn't just risk a bad session — it risks **stress fractures, prolapse, persistent incontinence, and pelvic pain** that can take months to resolve and sometimes don't fully resolve. These aren't theoretical risks; they're the modal outcomes for women who return to running too early. The cost of waiting 4–6 weeks longer than she wants is trivial. The cost of running too soon can be a year-long setback or permanent.

I'd say this to her plainly. She'll respect it.

## The Readiness Criteria

Before her first run — regardless of week number — she needs to pass a functional screen. The Goom/Donnelly criteria are the standard. She should be able to perform **all** of the following without symptoms (no leaking, no heaviness, no pain, no doming):

### Load and impact tolerance
- Walk 30 min briskly, symptom-free
- Single-leg balance, 10 sec each side
- Single-leg squat, 10 reps each side
- Single-leg bridge, 20 reps each side
- Single-leg calf raise, 20 reps each side
- Jog in place, 1 minute
- Forward bounds, 10 reps
- Hop in place on one leg, 10 reps each side
- Single-leg "running man" position hold, 10 sec each side

### Strength benchmarks (general targets)
- Squat: bodyweight or near it for 8 reps
- Deadlift/RDL: bodyweight for 8 reps
- Side plank: 30+ sec each side
- Single-leg work tolerated without compensation

### Pelvic floor and core
- No leaking with coughing, sneezing, jumping, or running in place
- No pelvic heaviness during or after activity
- DR generating tension across the linea alba, no doming under load
- Can perform a pelvic floor contraction *and* fully relax (relaxation is as important as contraction)

### Other markers
- Lochia fully stopped for several weeks
- No bleeding changes with increased activity
- Sleep averaging at least 5 hrs (broken is fine) over the prior 2 weeks — running on chronic severe sleep deprivation increases injury risk substantially
- Adequate energy availability — if breastfeeding, eating enough to support both lactation and training

**Pelvic floor PT assessment before first run is strongly recommended.** Not optional in my view, if access exists. It's the single highest-leverage thing you can do for her running future.

## How This Fits the Block You're Currently Running

The 4-week on-ramp she's in **already builds toward this.** Most of the criteria above are things she'll naturally develop through Weeks 2–4 (squat patterns, single-leg work, side planks, hinge strength). The Week 5–8 block I mentioned earlier is where we deliberately build the *impact* tolerance side of the screen.

## The Build to 10k — Week-by-Week Framework

Here's the structure I'd build her toward, assuming a clean Week 4 readiness assessment:

### Weeks 5–8: Impact Reintroduction (postpartum Weeks 14–18)
- Week 5: pogos, low-amplitude hops, double-leg landings from low step
- Week 6: single-leg hops, skater hops, jump squats (low amplitude), jumping jacks
- Week 7: single-leg landings, bounding, brief "jog in place" intervals (20–30 sec)
- Week 8: full readiness screen at end of week — pass = clear to start run/walk

Strength continues 2–3x/week through this block. Cardio is bike/rower/walking, building aerobic base for running without the impact.

### Weeks 9–12: Run/Walk Build (postpartum Weeks 18–22)
First runs are **never** continuous. The standard postpartum return uses run/walk intervals, building gradually.

- **Week 9:** 3 sessions of 1 min run / 2 min walk × 6 (~20 min total). Flat ground, soft surface if possible (grass, treadmill).
- **Week 10:** 2 min run / 2 min walk × 6
- **Week 11:** 3 min run / 1 min walk × 6
- **Week 12:** 5 min run / 1 min walk × 4

Strict rules during this phase:
- **Re-screen for symptoms after every session.** Leaking, heaviness, pelvic pain, midline doming on the next day's training — any of these = pause and reassess.
- **48 hours between runs minimum.** Run / strength / rest, run / strength / rest.
- **No back-to-back run days.**
- **Stop and walk if form degrades**, especially the moment her gait gets sloppy or she starts breath-holding.

### Weeks 13–18: Continuous Running Build (postpartum Weeks 22–28)
- Week 13: 2 × 10 min continuous, with walk break
- Week 14: 20 min continuous, easy pace
- Week 15: 25 min continuous
- Week 16: 30 min continuous
- Week 17: 35 min continuous + introduce one slightly longer weekend run
- Week 18: 40 min continuous + long run at 5k

Two runs/week through this phase, with the third optional. Strength stays at 2x/week.

### Weeks 19+: 10k-Specific Build (postpartum Week 28+)
This is where you can structure a proper 10k training block: long run, tempo, easy run, with the long run building 10% per week toward and through 10k distance. A 6–8 week build from being able to comfortably run 40 min should get her race-ready, assuming continued symptom-free progress.

**If she can run 40 min comfortably by postpartum Week 28** (~6.5 months PP), and we then run a 6–8 week 10k build, **she's race-ready around 8–9 months postpartum** — late October to mid-November if her baby was born in early March, for example. Adjust to her actual dates.

## The Strength Programme Doesn't Stop

This is the other thing to set expectations on with her now: she will be lifting **2x/week the entire time she's training for the 10k.** Postpartum runners who drop strength training to "focus on running" are the ones who get injured. The hip, glute, calf, and core strength built through your programming is what will let her run pain-free at 9 months PP and not develop the classic postpartum runner injuries (stress fractures, PGP, plantar fascia issues, recurring pelvic floor problems).

Frame it to her: **strength training is part of running training, not separate from it.**

## What to Do Right Now

In terms of how this affects the current block — nothing changes. Stay the course on the on-ramp. But you can start having the running conversation with her now so she's not blindsided by the timeline, and so she can:

1. **Book a pelvic floor PT assessment** for around postpartum Week 13–14, ahead of the impact reintroduction phase
2. **Pick a realistic race** — if she has one in mind already, look up the date and we can work backwards. If late October or later, brilliant. If September, we should pick a different race or step her down to a 5k for the first event back and put the 10k in early 2026.
3. **Sort her running kit** — properly fitted supportive sports bra (her bra size will likely have changed), and replace any shoes older than 6 months. Postpartum return is a good time for a gait assessment if she's ever wanted one.
4. **Manage expectations on pace.** Her first runs back will feel slow and effortful. Pre-pregnancy paces typically return 6–12 months after returning to running, not immediately. The goal of the first months is *time on feet without symptoms*, not pace.

## A Note on Breastfeeding and Running

If she's still breastfeeding when she returns to running:
- Feed or pump immediately before running — comfort and supply both benefit
- Hydration becomes more important, not less
- A second sports bra layer can help with comfort
- Some women notice supply dips with sudden training load increases — gradual progression protects this

## Summary for Her

- Earliest first run: ~6 weeks from now (Week 14 PP), and only if she passes the screen
- Realistic first run: 6–10 weeks from now
- 10k race ready: ~8–9 months postpartum if all goes well, so **late October at the earliest, more likely November**
- Pelvic floor PT assessment before first run is strongly advised
- Strength training continues throughout — it's not optional and not separate
- The 4 weeks of patience now buys her a running career, not just one race

Want me to draft the Week 5–8 impact reintroduction block in detail so you've got it ready to roll into? That's the block that bridges where she is now to her first run, and it's worth getting right.

# 4-Week Postpartum On-Ramp Block (Weeks 10–14 Postpartum) — Consolidated

## Client Context

- 10 weeks postpartum, OB cleared for moderate exercise, no jumping until ~Week 14 PP
- Continuing from earlier 4-week postpartum foundation block
- Spin background, wants cardio and eventually HIIT
- Autumn 10k goal — running return planned for Week 14+ PP, separate block
- Home setup with light DBs (5/10/15 lb), chair, mat, wall
- Stationary bike available

## Programme Principles

1. Continue breath-to-pelvic-floor connection under load
2. Screen DR formally at Week 1, Week 3, end of Week 4 — visually every session
3. Build tissue tolerance gradually; no impact, no Valsalva, no spinal flexion under load
4. Reintroduce hinge, squat, push, pull, carry patterns under progressive load
5. Anti-flexion core (anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion) only — no crunches
6. Cardio progresses from steady to intervals to postpartum-appropriate conditioning circuits
7. Fat loss is **not** the goal of this block; recovery, capacity, and tissue tolerance are
8. Stop signs every session: coning/doming, pelvic heaviness, leaking, low back pain, bleeding changes, mastitis flare

## Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Strength Day 1 (Lower + Core) |
| Tue | Steady bike |
| Wed | Strength Day 2 (Upper + Carries) |
| Thu | Easy walk 20–30 min |
| Fri | Strength Day 3 (Full Body) |
| Sat | Conditioning (steady bike Wks 1–2 → intervals Wk 3 → circuit Wks 3–4) |
| Sun | Rest |

Session length 30–40 min. Cardio sessions 20–30 min.

---

## WEEK 1 — Acclimatisation

Goal: structured movement re-exposure, recalibrate exertion, confirm symptom-free tolerance. RPE 4–5. Long rests. No DBs heavier than 5 lb.

**Baseline DR screen on Day 1 before any training.** Document gap width and depth at three points (above navel, at navel, below navel) and tension quality with the brace test.

### Day 1 (Mon) — Movement Screen + Reconnection
- 360° breathing, supine, 2 × 8 breaths
- Heel slides with exhale on effort, 2 × 6/side
- Bodyweight glute bridge, 2 × 8 — watch for doming
- Bodyweight box squat to chair, 2 × 8
- Wall push-up, 2 × 8
- Side-lying clamshell, 2 × 10/side
- Dead bug, heels only, 2 × 6/side
- Finish: 5 min slow walk + diaphragmatic breathing

**Core finisher:** 90/90 supine breathing 2 × 6 breaths, dead bug 2 × 6/side, side-lying oblique breathing 1 × 5/side

### Day 2 (Tue) — Steady Bike
- 15 min, RPE 4, conversational, flat resistance, 80–90 rpm
- Confirm no symptoms: leaking, heaviness, perineal soreness, scar pulling

### Day 3 (Wed) — Light Patterning
- Cat-cow, 1 × 8
- Hip hinge to wall, bodyweight, 2 × 8
- Suitcase hold, 5 lb, 2 × 20 sec/side
- Tall-kneeling overhead press, 5 lb, 2 × 8
- Bird dog, slow, exhale on extension, 2 × 6/side
- Standing single-arm row, 5 lb, 2 × 10
- Finish: child's pose, 90/90 hip switches × 6

**Core finisher:** Bird dog 2 × 6/side, Pallof press (band or 5 lb at chest) 2 × 8/side, wall plank 2 × 20 sec

### Day 4 (Thu) — Easy Walk
20–30 min, flat, conversational

### Day 5 (Fri) — Mini Full-Body
- Goblet squat to chair, 5 lb, 2 × 8
- Incline push-up (counter/chair), 2 × 6
- Standing single-arm row, 5 lb, 2 × 8/side
- Glute bridge with march, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 15 sec/side
- Finish: 10 min walk

**Core finisher:** Side plank from knees 2 × 15 sec/side, dead bug 2 × 6/side, suitcase hold 5 lb 2 × 20 sec/side

### Day 6 (Sat) — Walk
20–30 min easy

### Day 7 — Rest

**End of Week 1 check-in:** symptoms? sleep? energy? bleeding changes? Use this to decide whether Week 2 progresses as written or repeats Week 1 patterns.

---

## WEEK 2 — Build Movement Quality Under Load

Goal: A/B split with proper structure, modest load progression to 10 lb early, **mid-week intensity bump introduced if she's feeling good and symptom-free.** RPE 5–6 first half, building to 6 second half.

### Day 1 (Mon) — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet box squat, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- DB RDL, 10 lb each, 3 × 8 (exhale on the way up, no breath-holding)
- Reverse lunge, bodyweight or 5 lb, 2 × 6/side
- Glute bridge, 2 × 12
- Dead bug with arm reach, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 20 sec/side

**Core finisher:** Dead bug with arm reach 3 × 6/side, side plank from knees 2 × 20 sec/side, bird dog with 2-sec pause 2 × 8/side

### Day 2 (Tue) — Steady Bike
20–25 min, RPE 5, conversational

### Day 3 (Wed) — Upper + Carries (B) — *mid-week progression*
- DB floor press, 12 lb, 3 × 8 *(progressed from 10)*
- Single-arm bent-over row, 12 lb, 3 × 10/side *(progressed)*
- Half-kneeling overhead press, 10 lb, 3 × 8/side *(extra set)*
- Suitcase carry, 12 lb, 3 × 40 sec/side *(progressed)*
- Wall slide / scap retraction, 2 × 10
- Bird dog, 2 × 8/side, 2-sec pause at extension

**Core finisher:** Half-kneeling Pallof press 3 × 8/side, bear hold 2 × 15 sec, suitcase carry 10 lb 2 × 30 sec/side

### Day 4 (Thu) — Easy Walk
20–30 min

### Day 5 (Fri) — Full Body (revised)
- Goblet squat, 12 lb, 3 × 8 *(extra set, modest load bump)*
- Incline push-up, slightly lower surface, 3 × 8 *(complexity, not load)*
- DB RDL, 12 lb, 3 × 10
- Single-arm row, 12 lb, 3 × 10/side
- Pallof press, 3 × 10/side with 2-sec hold at extension
- 10–15 min brisk walk

**Core finisher:** Side plank from knees with reach-through 2 × 6/side, dead bug opposite arm + leg 2 × 6/side, Pallof press hold 2 × 20 sec/side

### Day 6 (Sat) — Bike Intervals
- 5 min warm-up RPE 3–4
- 8 × (1 min RPE 6 / 1 min easy RPE 4) *(progressed from 6 rounds)*
- 5 min cool-down
- Total: ~26 min

### Day 7 — Rest

## WEEK 3 — Progress Load, Pattern Complexity, Conditioning Format

Goal: Real load bump (15 lb on hinges/carries), introduce split-stance work, swap bike intervals for first **postpartum-appropriate conditioning circuit**. RPE 6–7. Still no jumping, no flexion under load, no plank from toes unless DR closed and tension generation is good.

### Day 1 (Mon) — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet squat, 12–15 lb, 3 × 8
- DB RDL, 15 lb each, 3 × 8 *(real load bump on the safest pattern)*
- Split squat, 5–10 lb DBs, 2 × 8/side
- Glute bridge with 10 lb on hips, 3 × 10
- Dead bug with opposite arm + leg, 2 × 6/side
- Side plank from knees, 2 × 25 sec/side

**Core finisher:** Dead bug with 5 lb DB in straight arms 3 × 6/side, side plank with top leg lift 2 × 8/side, bird dog 3 × 8/side

### Day 2 (Tue) — Steady Bike
25–30 min, RPE 5–6

### Day 3 (Wed) — Upper + Carries (B)
- DB floor press, 12 lb, 3 × 10
- Chest-supported row (over chair/bench), 12 lb, 3 × 10
- Standing overhead press, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- Suitcase carry, 15 lb, 3 × 45 sec/side
- Bent-over reverse fly, 5 lb, 2 × 10
- Bird dog, 2 × 8/side, slowed tempo

**Core finisher:** Tall-kneeling Pallof press 3 × 10/side, bear hold with shoulder tap 2 × 6/side, single-arm farmer carry 12 lb 3 × 40 sec/side

### Day 4 (Thu) — Easy Walk
20–30 min

**DR re-screen this week** — schedule before or after this day. Document changes from baseline.

### Day 5 (Fri) — Full Body Circuit
3 rounds, 90 sec rest between rounds:
- Goblet squat × 8 (12 lb)
- Push-up (incline as needed) × 8
- DB RDL × 8 (12 lb)
- Single-arm row × 8/side (12 lb)
- Pallof press × 8/side

**Core finisher:** Side plank from knees 2 × 30 sec/side, bird dog row 5 lb 2 × 6/side, half-kneeling chop (band or light DB) 2 × 8/side

### Day 6 (Sat) — Conditioning Circuit (replaces bike intervals)
5 min easy bike/walk warm-up.

3 rounds, 30 sec work / 30 sec rest:
1. Goblet squat, 12 lb
2. Single-arm row, 12 lb (switch sides each round)
3. Reverse lunge, alternating, bodyweight or 5 lb
4. Half-kneeling DB push press, 8–10 lb (switch sides each round)
5. Farmer carry, 12 lb each hand, walking
6. Bike sprint, seated, RPE 7

**Stop the circuit immediately** if doming, leaking, or heaviness appears.

### Day 7 — Rest

## WEEK 4 — Consolidate and Test Readiness for Impact

Goal: confirm load tolerance, introduce impact *precursors* (no actual jumps yet), and run the readiness assessment at end of week to clear her for the Week 5–8 impact block. RPE 6–7.

### Day 1 (Mon) — Lower + Core (A)
- Goblet squat, 15 lb, 4 × 8
- DB RDL, 15 lb each, 4 × 8
- Split squat, 10 lb DBs, 3 × 8/side
- Step-up to low step, 10 lb, 2 × 8/side
- Heel raises (calf prep for landing), 3 × 12
- Side plank from knees with top leg lift, 2 × 8/side
- Dead bug, 2 × 8/side

**Core finisher:** Dead bug with 8–10 lb DB 3 × 8/side, side plank from feet (only if DR closed and tension good — otherwise stay on knees 30 sec) 2 × 20 sec/side, bird dog with 2-sec pause 3 × 8/side

### Day 2 (Tue) — Steady Bike
30 min, RPE 6

### Day 3 (Wed) — Upper + Carries (B)
- DB floor press, 15 lb, 4 × 8
- Single-arm row, 15 lb, 4 × 8/side
- Standing OH press, 10 lb, 3 × 8
- Farmer carry (both hands), 15 lb each, 3 × 45 sec
- Half-kneeling Pallof, 3 × 8/side
- Bird dog row, 8–10 lb, 2 × 6/side

**Core finisher:** Half-kneeling Pallof with slow tempo (3 sec out / 1 sec hold / 3 sec in) 3 × 8/side, bear crawl forward + back 2 × 4 steps each, farmer carry 15 lb each 3 × 45 sec

### Day 4 (Thu) — Easy Walk
20–30 min

### Day 5 (Fri) — Full Body + Impact Prep
- Goblet squat, 15 lb, 3 × 10
- Push-up (knees or full if DR closed), 3 × 6–8
- DB RDL, 15 lb, 3 × 10
- Single-arm row, 15 lb, 3 × 10/side

**Impact prep block (no jumping yet):**
- Marching in place, 2 × 30 sec
- Heel raise to forefoot hop *simulation* (stay on ground, fast contraction), 2 × 10
- Fast step-back to lunge (no bounce), 2 × 6/side

- Pallof press, 2 × 10/side

**Core finisher:** Side plank with small hip dip 2 × 8/side, bird dog row 8 lb 3 × 8/side, tall-kneeling anti-rotation hold 2 × 20 sec/side

### Day 6 (Sat) — Progressed Conditioning Circuit
5 min warm-up.

4 rounds, 40 sec work / 20 sec rest:
1. Goblet squat, 15 lb
2. DB push press, 10 lb (alternating arms standing, or both arms if symptom-free)
3. DB step-up to low step, 10 lb (alternating)
4. Single-arm row, 15 lb (alternating)
5. Suitcase carry, 15 lb (switch sides each round)
6. Bike or rower, RPE 7–8

Rest 90 sec between rounds. 5 min cool-down. Total ~30 min, RPE peaks at 7–8. Closest she'll get to "real" HIIT this block.

### Day 7 — Rest + End-of-Block Assessment

## End-of-Block Readiness Assessment (End of Week 4)

Run the DR screen one final time and check the following:

**Symptom-free across the block:**
- No leaking during conditioning, carries, or fast marches
- No pelvic heaviness during or after sessions
- No coning/doming under load
- No bleeding changes
- No persistent low back or SI pain

**DR screen:**
- Gap unchanged or narrower from baseline
- Tension across linea alba good (taut, not squishy) at all three points
- No doming when she lifts head with brace strategy

**Load benchmarks:**
- Goblet squat 15 lb × 10, clean
- DB RDL 15 lb × 10, clean
- Single-arm row 15 lb × 10/side, clean
- Farmer carry 15 lb each, 45 sec, upright posture
- Dead bug 10 lb DB × 8/side, no doming
- Side plank from knees 30 sec/side, ideally from feet 20 sec/side if appropriate

**Other markers:**
- Walking 30+ min symptom-free
- Sleep and energy trending up across the block, not down
- Sustained 3 sessions/week + 2 cardio + 1 walk without flagging

**Pass = clear to start Week 5–8 impact reintroduction block.**
**Partial pass = hold for 1–2 more weeks at Week 4 prescription.**
**Any fails on the DR screen or symptom items = pelvic floor PT referral before continuing.**

# 4-Week Postpartum On-Ramp Block (Weeks 10–14 Postpartum) — Consolidated

## Client Context

- 10 weeks postpartum, OB cleared for moderate exercise, no jumping until ~Week 14 PP
- Continuing from earlier 4-week postpartum foundation block
- Spin background, wants cardio and eventually HIIT
- Autumn 10k goal — running return planned for Week 14+ PP, separate block
- Home setup with light DBs (5/10/15 lb), chair, mat, wall
- Stationary bike available

## Programme Principles

1. Continue breath-to-pelvic-floor connection under load
2. Screen DR formally at Week 1, Week 3, end of Week 4 — visually every session
3. Build tissue tolerance gradually; no impact, no Valsalva, no spinal flexion under load
4. Reintroduce hinge, squat, push, pull, carry patterns under progressive load
5. Anti-flexion core (anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion) only — no crunches
6. Cardio progresses from steady to intervals to postpartum-appropriate conditioning circuits
7. Fat loss is **not** the goal of this block; recovery, capacity, and tissue tolerance are
8. Stop signs every session: coning/doming, pelvic heaviness, leaking, low back pain, bleeding changes, mastitis flare

## Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Strength Day 1 (Lower + Core) |
| Tue | Steady bike |
| Wed | Strength Day 2 (Upper + Carries) |
| Thu | Easy walk 20–30 min |
| Fri | Strength Day 3 (Full Body) |
| Sat | Conditioning (steady bike Wks 1–2 → intervals Wk 3 → circuit Wks 3–4) |
| Sun | Rest |

Session length 30–40 min. Cardio sessions 20–30 min.

---

## WEEK 1 — Acclimatisation

Goal: structured movement re-exposure, recalibrate exertion, confirm symptom-free tolerance. RPE 4–5. Long rests. No DBs heavier than 5 lb.

**Baseline DR screen on Day 1 before any training.** Document gap width and depth at three points (above navel, at navel, below navel) and tension quality with the brace test.

### Day 1 (Mon) — Movement Screen + Reconnection
- 360° breathing, supine, 2 × 8 breaths
- Heel slides with exhale on effort, 2 × 6/side
- Bodyweight glute bridge, 2 × 8 — watch for doming
- Bodyweight box squat to chair, 2 × 8
- Wall push-up, 2 × 8
- Side-lying clamshell, 2 × 10/side
- Dead bug, heels only, 2 × 6/side
- Finish: 5 min slow walk + diaphragmatic breathing

**Core finisher:** 90/90 supine breathing 2 × 6 breaths, dead bug 2 × 6/side, side-lying oblique breathing 1 × 5/side

### Day 2 (Tue) — Steady Bike
- 15 min, RPE 4, conversational, flat resistance, 80–90 rpm
- Confirm no symptoms: leaking, heaviness, perineal soreness, scar pulling

### Day 3 (Wed) — Light Patterning

## End-of-Block Readiness Assessment (End of Week 4)

Run the DR screen one final time and check the following:

**Symptom-free across the block:**
- No leaking during conditioning, carries, or fast marches
- No pelvic heaviness during or after sessions
- No coning/doming under load
- No bleeding changes
- No persistent low back or SI pain

**DR screen:**
- Gap unchanged or narrower from baseline
- Tension across linea alba good (taut, not squishy) at all three points
- No doming when she lifts head with brace strategy

**Load benchmarks:**
- Goblet squat 15 lb × 10, clean
- DB RDL 15 lb × 10, clean
- Single-arm row 15 lb × 10/side, clean
- Farmer carry 15 lb each, 45 sec, upright posture
- Dead bug 10 lb DB × 8/side, no doming
- Side plank from knees 30 sec/side, ideally from feet 20 sec/side if appropriate

**Other markers:**
- Walking 30+ min symptom-free
- Sleep and energy trending up across the block, not down
- Sustained 3 sessions/week + 2 cardio + 1 walk without flagging

**Pass = clear to start Week 5–8 impact reintroduction block.**
**Partial pass = hold for 1–2 more weeks at Week 4 prescription.**
**Any fails on the DR screen or symptom items = pelvic floor PT referral before continuing.**

## Recovery, Nutrition, and Lifestyle

- **Walks:** Thursday + as much general walking as feasible. Steps drive postpartum recovery more than any other modifiable variable.
- **Sleep:** brutal at this stage. If she had <5 hrs broken sleep, drop sets to 2 of each, shorten session to 20 min — don't cancel, downscale.
- **Hydration:** 3+ L/day, more if breastfeeding.
- **Nutrition:** protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg goal bodyweight. **Not a fat loss block.** No deliberate deficit if breastfeeding. If she pushes on fat loss, redirect to protein, steps, and patience — body composition shifts will follow training and time.
